I wish there was a neutral option on Steam for reviews, but honestly, I cannot see what the hype is about on Celeste. The music and atmosphere is done beautifully, but when you get to the core gameplay and it's mechanics, that's where it falls off hard for me. This game is the first one on Steam that I've requested a refund for because of how little fun I had in chapters 1, 2 and the bit of 3 that I did. Coming from both Hollow Knight games, and surprisingly Deltarune Chapter 5, this does not feel good to control at all. Madeline is very heavy and feels like she falls way too fast, and the reliance on the dash makes platforming unnecessarily difficult. Wall Jumping is something that shouldn't be that difficult to understand, but with the looseness of the control, it was impossible to do consistently. Maybe this is a skill issue on my part, but the game doesn't feel fun enough to warrant keeping it even if I did buy it for five dollars.

Awesome art, but the controls only work very well on controller.
Overall a very good game

claims.claim: The game features an assist mode that allows players to adjust difficulty settings such as speed or invincibility.

citations.review_text: I love this game! I I've only been Chapter 4A so far but it's been amazing. Challenging, but amazing. The simple movement mechanics are very fluid (unless you're me and can't aim your dashes half the time), and each chapter's gimmick make every one of them unique. The story I've seen so far is amazing, and from what I've heard, if gets even better. 10/10 if you love precision platformers. And even if you just like causal, you can turn on assist mode and still get everything :3

Celeste is a weird game for me: It's a gorgeous game both visually and soundtrack-wise, helped with a wonderful small story of mental health, something I can definitely see why people call it a masterpiece. The platforming is simple but strong, with a good challenge to it.

But it's also a game that I find the difficulty goes from challenging to frustrating down to annoying for me. Maybe it is just a skill issue but by around the fourth chapter does the game get too difficult for me to get through it normally. Especially if you wanna try the collectibles.
[i]But[/i] at the same time the game never really hinders you either. Assist mode exists and makes it as hard or easy as you need it to be, from slowing the game down, extra boosts to just invincibility. So completion isn't impossible if you suck at these harder platformers.

So see this review as a "not for me, but still recommended by being quite forgiving".

Celeste is really pretty and Its so cutesy and i love it it makes my jellies fluttery but its also hard for the sake of being hard for people that like making things harder for the sake of making them harder but it has a assist mode and it'd also just a really wholesome storyline while being a fulfilling and satisfying platformer.

The difficulty is the obvious entry point. Celeste is hard in a way that feels fair rather than punishing, death is instant and the respawn is instant, and the loop of attempting a screen, dying, learning, clearing it has a rhythm that pulls you forward rather than pushing you away. Assist mode existing without judgment for people who want a different experience is a design decision more games should make.

The mountain as a metaphor for mental health and anxiety is where the game does its most interesting work narratively. Madeline's internal struggle externalizes itself through the game's mechanics in ways that feel genuinely considered rather than bolted on, and the emotional beats land harder because the platforming is earning them rather than just decorating around them.

The soundtrack from Lena Raine is exceptional. The kind of music that would work completely outside the game context and is elevated further by being inside it.

Whatever your feelings on the creator's personal story and how much of it you think belongs in the game, the mechanics and the level design and the core experience stand completely on their own terms. One of the best platformers made in the last decade by any measure you want to apply to it.

claims.claim: The game includes a modding scene and extra content available after finishing the main chapters.

citations.review_text: I played this on Playstation first and just got it on PC. This game is almost certainly THE greatest platformer of all time. I've recommended it to everyone I know and everyone who's gotten it has loved it. And there's tons of extra content after the game finishes in the form of mods, and it's also very replayable. Totally recommend.

Played it so many times on my switch before but finally decided to beat all the C-Sides plus Farewell legit this time around and honestly was one of the best feelings i've ever had while playing a game and that's gotta mean something. Personally my favourite platformer ever made and i can't ever see it getting topped.

Also even with the base game done i totally recommend looking into the modding scene so many wonderful creators around and endless hours of more celeste content just waiting to be played (Strawberry Jam is a must play)

Be careful! If you've downloaded Celeste on itch.io or a different method, and try to play the game through Steam, it will overwrite your first save file! I nearly lost my original save file with around 190 strawberries unlocked, luckily I could restore it with the backups the devs had the insight to set up.

That being said, this is a game worth buying twice. The first time, I purchased Celeste through an itch.io bundle at a steep discount, but I love this game so dearly I bought it again here to officially unlock all the achievements. My real playtime is more than 300 hours. Snappy, satisfying gameplay, gorgeous pixel art, a thriving mod community, I'm sure it's all been said at this point. Fantastic game. But BE CAREFUL with those save files.

Honestly I would recommend this game, If it wasn't for the final chapter.
And to preface this, I beat it. I beat farewell. And I also got the wow berry which is an optional extra challenge on top of the farewell chapter, just to prove I'm good at the game and not just skill issuing this.

The difficulty spike is just beyond unreasonable. The final chapter was basically designed to challenge speed runners instead of the average player. Requiring completion of what was previously optional challenges, and learning what used to be a speed run glitch to complete. It's just simply, unfair. Unfair to a degree that no other challenging game that isn't deliberately a rage game or just total slop can boast. And the chapter opens in such a way that it guilts you for not finishing it. It's BS. I completed it, and it's BS. Made me give up on the game for several years before giving it a second shot. Older, calmer, better at games, having completed several highly challenging games since, and I say with absolute conviction that the final chapter in this game is just downright not okay. If I wasn't unreasonably stubborn about stuff like this I would have dropped the game for good. So the fact I dropped it for several years over this should be telling.

I got a lot of hard games under my belt at this point and absolutely nothing comes close. This is a level of difficulty that should be reserved for mods. Or at the very least an optional challenge instead of a story chapter.

The rest of the game? Great. Fantastic, even. But Farewell just takes all of the enjoyment you felt up to that point, crams it in a sack, and repeatedly bashes you in the balls with it.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as extremely challenging, particularly in late-game content such as the B-sides, C-sides, and the final chapter.

citations.review_text:
The Bottom Line
Celeste is a phenomenal, top-tier platformer that will take you to absolute mountain peaks of satisfaction—and then beat you right down into the valleys of frustration. It’s essentially the Dark Souls of precision platformers: punishing, relentless, but insanely rewarding if you have the grit to stick it out. Doing a full 100% run—all A/B/C-Sides, Chapter 9 Farewell, and the Moon Berry—without ever touching Assist Mode is a brutal test of endurance, but crossing that finish line on pure execution alone is a genuine badge of honor.

(Also, for anyone turned off by online claims calling this a "woke" game or bringing up post-launch dev commentary about Madeline: rest assured that none of that exists inside the actual game. There are no shoehorned political themes or overt references in the story—it is purely a focused, personal narrative about overcoming mental hurdles and climbing a mountain.)

The Crunch
The gameplay mechanics are tight, responsive, and deterministic. For 90% of the game, every screen feels like a brilliant physics puzzle where you identify the path, time your dashes, and execute. However, as you dive into the late B-Sides, C-Sides, and Farewell, the design pivots hard into extreme execution strain and sub-pixel precision. Tech like hyper-dashes, wall-bounces, and jellyfish momentum carries demand frame-tight inputs. When you're mid-air during a long sequence, missing a grab by a millisecond will rocket you straight into spikes, making a few late-game rooms feel more like luck and endurance than puzzle-solving. But when a run finally clicks, the feeling of mastery is unmatched.

The Flow
The pacing of the main story (A-Sides) is near-perfect, gradually teaching you advanced movement while introducing unique mechanics for each chapter. The collectibles—strawberries and cassette tapes—are genuinely fun side-puzzles to hunt down. The real trial begins after the credits roll. The B and C-Sides condense levels into high-density g…

claims.claim: Reviewers report that dying does not feel punishing because respawns and screen transitions are fast and failure functions as a learning tool.

citations.review_text:
Very fun; the controls start out weird if you're not used to Z, X, C and arrow keys (like me), but you get super used to it at around chapter 4. Also really nice to play casually since dying isn't punishing at all. 
The music is amazing and so is the atmosphere, absolutely worth playing even if you don't make it far.

This is a good game. Before talking about the gameplay, let me say that the music is very good, the story is enjoyable, and the art is absolutely amazing. This is one of the best-looking games I've ever played. This is really one of those games that prove that a game can look awesome without having "realistic" graphics. 
Now, for the gameplay. It is very good. Your control of the movement is very accurate and isn't buggy, and it never feels like the game just didn't function well when you fail. This is one of those games where you repeatedly try to beat something for a very long time, and eventually succeed. By that, I mean that in each level (which is an entire area), you have many screens (I don't know if there's an actual name for them, so that's how I'll call them). Each screen is a small part of the level, that you need to pass to get further in the level (usually it will just be getting from one side to the other). Now, a successful run through any screen will usually only take a few seconds. But the thing is that you'll try each screen dozens of times, unless you're replaying an old level. And that's the point. You can try as many times as you want, and there's no punishment to failing. Once you complete a screen, you move on to the next. There are usually between 10 to 30 screens per area if I'm not mistaken (I might be mistaken). You just have to try enough times to succeed. There aren't any upgrades or anything like that, so your success is entirely dependent on your skill. I mean, there is one thing you unlock in further levels, but you don't have it in the earlier levels and it just lets the game developers give you harder challenges to overcome.
There isn't really RNG - there are some levels with moving objects, so you might feel like getting to them at the right moment is RNG. But since they start in the exact same position every time, eventually you just enter a rhythm and get to the same exact position in the same exact time, and figure out how to …

I got this game because it was a platformer based on Mountain climbing
I finished the game in 90 hours because the story and music are absolutely peak (pun intended)
I continued playing because it's a platformer based on Mountain climbing and there are a ton of modded maps to still climb

This is my favourite game. It's a neat package of many elements done exceptionally well.

The thing making me come back to it is how fluid the movement system is with so 'little' movement options. Still, after all these hours, it is fun to jump and dash around all the levels - and if they get a bit stale, there is always the option of trying out some of the amazing mods the community has made (the community is one of the most prolific out there).

Back to the game, the gameplay is about precisely platforming (...) and figuring how to do so with limited resources - there are many ways in which any given room can be solved. The game places emphasis on exploration, not only in movement options - how you approach a room, etc. - but also in how you go about moving through the bigger sandbox - the chapter you are currently in. Throughout all of the levels, there are many hidden things you are not forced to interact with, that offer a greater challenge than the base chapter itself. 

The music is composed by Lena Raine (most known for Celeste and Minecraft). It sets the atmosphere of every level nicely and during the more tense parts, it gets you moving fasstt. It is one of my favourite OSTs - years after playing Celeste for the first time and after brushing off the feelings accompanying someone post beating a game they really liked, I quite often find myself listening to some of the tracks from it.

The story is about facing personal struggles - without going in too deep - it is nice. It did get me emotional at times. 

This is a must-play for people who enjoy games based on fluid movement and for those who want to challenge themselves.
wonderful modding scene, after hundreds of hours playing the immense variety of what people have made I just keep falling more and more in love with this game

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game has very short room lengths and quick, painless respawns upon death.

citations.review_text:
I'll be honest.
This game puts before you an obstacle and tell you to get past it.
It tells you to figure out what you need to do and do it, even if you find it hard.
It expects you to figure things out yourself, with most tutorials consisting of telling you what buttons to press.

Yet it also knows what you should be capable of.
It knows what you've done before and gives you something just out of reach at your skill level, then puts that something in a perfect environment for learning it.
If you're willing to concede on your ego, it gives you tools to make it easier. Yeah, it might not be the intended experience, but it still is an experience.

And what I think is most important, it doesn't judge you for failing.
You will die, and the game understands that. So it makes death painless. If you mess up, you try again, no fuss.

Thank you, Maddy.
You taught me patience.
You taught me perseverance.
You taught me failure is a natural part of learning.


And to anyone thinking of buying the game, please, PLEASE, know that there is no shame in turning on assist mode. If you don't want to use it to skip the room, use it to learn the room. Skip to the parts that you find hard and practice them. Slow the game down to figure out what to do. Then try the room from start to finish. The game has more to offer than you will lose from slightly compromising on your ego.

Não sei muito bem como descrever celeste, considerando que foi meu primeiro plataforma que zerei e platinei

Mais sinceramente foi um ótimo jogo que me divertir muito, mesmo não sendo muito bom no jogo ainda assim consegui platinar, e agora entendo porque o chamam de "o jogo mais difícil que quer que você tenha sucesso", apesar de difícil o jogo não e nem um pouquinho punitivo,  sendo bem generoso com os checkpoints e com as telas de morte que duram meio segundo

Alem disso a curva de aprendizado do jogo e ótima, aonde quando você morre a culpa não e do jogo mais sim sua, tanto que muitas vezes você sabe o movimento que precisa fazer e mesmo assim vai lá e da o pior pulo possível e morre do lado do checkpoint (experiência própria).E também vale ressaltar para os platinadores, o jogo não possui nenhuma conquista absurda, e mesmo se você tiver dificuldade pode usar o modo assistente que deixa o jogo mais facil, mais claro que ai perde a essência

Bem concluindo, foi um ótimo jogo, difícil mais justo, que me divertiu bastante e fico feliz que esse tenha sido o primeiro jogo plataforma que zerei e platinei

My genuine favorite video game of all time  (no spoilers in this review)

At the time of writing this I have every steam achievement and working on 100%ing it (maybe one day). A mountain on the heart... 2,000 meters and just as many ways to die. Celeste is honestly one of the best 2D platformers I've ever played. It's a profoundly honest game, built around an obvious yet powerful metaphor: climbing a mountain to find yourself.

The player controls Madeline, who, judging by the chara-design, could be mistaken for a young girl, but is actually 21 years old and sets out to reach the mountain's summit. During her ascent, Madeline will encounter several secondary characters, such as Theo, a social media addict who would risk his life for a dangerous selfie, a little old lady who lives at the foot of the hill and will undoubtedly make fun of us, the ghost of Mr. Oshiro, a former manager of a mountain hotel, and our evil twin "Badeline", who will be unleashed in the mirror temple.

At first glance, the game seems quite classic, a "die and retry" type of gameplay, but what can I say? The visual design is so beautiful, the controls are really good, both on keyboard and controller. Each chapter has its own unique atmosphere, evoking so much emotion, all enhanced by the splendid music by Lena Raine.

Want an extra challenge? Strawberry collecting is here (it's much more complicated than it looks) the B-sides and the C-sides are there for you and are completely optional. So, if you're playing casually, there's no need to grind the levels: just let the game guide you, it does that very well. Moreover, for those who want an even more relaxed experience, there's even an assist mode to help you if you're struggling a bit too much.

It's hard not to fall under the charm of this adventure and its heroine, Madeline, who confronts her depression, metaphorically represented by Mount Celeste. Despite the rage this game gave me in certain places, I could only hold on, give it my all and start over again and again, so strong was the desire to see her succeed.

Celeste is a must-play. I encourage everyone, even those unfamiliar with this type of game, to try it. …
